clinicalPearls: The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, defined by arthritis beginning before 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks, with other causes excluded.
It is a heterogeneous group of subtypes, including oligoarticular, polyarticular, systemic, enthesitis-related, and psoriatic forms, each with distinct features and prognosis.
Arthritis presents with joint swelling, morning stiffness or gelling, and limited movement, often with less pain than expected; young children may present with limp or refusal to use a limb.
Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype, typically affecting large joints in young girls and carrying a significant risk of chronic anterior uveitis.
Uveitis is frequently asymptomatic, so regular ophthalmological slit-lamp screening is essential to prevent visual loss, particularly in young ANA-positive children.
Systemic JIA features prominent extra-articular disease with quotidian high fever, an evanescent salmon-coloured rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis.
The diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion; laboratory tests support rather than confirm it, and inflammatory markers may be normal in oligoarticular disease.
A serious complication of systemic JIA is macrophage activation syndrome, a form of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that can be rapidly fatal.
Management principles combine anti-inflammatory therapy, disease-modifying agents, and increasingly biologic therapy, alongside physiotherapy to preserve joint function and growth.
reference.pathophysiology: JIA results from immune dysregulation leading to chronic inflammation of the synovium. In most subtypes, an aberrant adaptive immune response with T-cell activation and autoantibody production drives synovial proliferation (pannus), which can erode cartilage and bone and disturb the growth of nearby physes. Systemic JIA is instead an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by the innate immune system and proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, accounting for its prominent systemic features and its predisposition to macrophage activation syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive and post-infectious arthritis (including acute rheumatic fever)
Leukaemia and other malignancy presenting with bone or joint pain
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases
Non-inflammatory causes such as trauma, hypermobility, and benign limb pains
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, ESR, and C-reactive protein
Antinuclear antibody (informs uveitis risk) and rheumatoid factor
Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination for uveitis screening
Joint imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to assess synovitis and effusion
Ferritin, triglycerides, and fibrinogen if macrophage activation syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome (persistent fever, falling cell counts, very high ferritin, hepatic dysfunction)
Findings suggesting malignancy such as severe night pain, cytopenias, or systemic decline
A hot, acutely swollen joint with fever suggesting septic arthritis
Visual symptoms or complications of uveitis
Systemic features such as high spiking fever with serositis
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies by subtype; many children with oligoarticular disease do well, while polyarticular and systemic forms may follow a more persistent course, and modern therapy has substantially improved remission rates and reduced long-term joint damage. Uveitis and macrophage activation syndrome remain important causes of morbidity.
pitfalls: Missing asymptomatic uveitis by omitting scheduled slit-lamp screening
Overlooking leukaemia in a child with bone pain and abnormal counts before starting steroids
Failing to recognise early macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA
Attributing a single hot joint to JIA and missing septic arthritis
management: Use non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for initial symptom control of active arthritis
Give intra-articular corticosteroid injections, particularly effective in oligoarticular disease
Start methotrexate as the first-line disease-modifying drug for polyarticular and persistent disease
Escalate to biologics, using TNF inhibitors for polyarticular disease and IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors for systemic JIA
Undertake regular slit-lamp ophthalmology screening and treat chronic anterior uveitis to prevent visual loss
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve joint function and growth
Recognise and treat macrophage activation syndrome urgently in systemic JIA with anakinra and corticosteroids
